Often, yes. Gum disease is very common in older pets, especially small dogs. Signs include:
- Bad breath that doesn't go away
- Red or swollen gums
- Trouble picking up, chewing or swallowing food

Bad breath can also point to other illness. A sweet smell may mean diabetes, and a urine-like smell may mean kidney disease.

See your vet for a mouth check. Proper cleaning below the gumline needs anesthesia. Vets check older pets carefully first, and treating mouth pain often makes them much happier.

At home, brush your pet's teeth with pet toothpaste, never human toothpaste. See a vet soon if your pet stops eating or has a lump in the mouth.

Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if he has more than one in a row, or if he might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Yes, treat this as an emergency. For cats, every part of true lilies and daylilies is poisonous, including the pollen and the vase water. Even a small amount licked off the fur can cause deadly kidney failure. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Early treatment makes a big difference. Waiting 18 hours or more often leads to kidney damage that can't be reversed.

Before you go:
- Wipe the pollen off her fur with a damp cloth so she can't lick more.
- Bring the flower or a photo so the vet can identify it.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

She may look fine at first. Early signs include drooling, vomiting, low energy and not eating. Keep lilies out of homes with cats.

Please don't wait for signs. Raisins and grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, so treat any amount seriously. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Vomiting or diarrhea often starts within 6 to 12 hours. Later signs include low energy, not eating, belly pain, weakness and drinking a lot. Kidney failure can develop within 1 to 3 days, and it is often fatal.

Before you go:
- Bring the bread or packaging so the vet can estimate how many raisins he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and note any vomiting or diarrhea to tell the vet.

Still go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) promptly after washing the wound. The health workers there will look at the bite and the dog's vaccination record and decide what treatment you need.

Don't skip the visit or wait for the dog to finish its 14-day observation first. DOH offices urge immediate consultation after any bite or scratch, because rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear.

Bring the dog's vaccination card or a photo of it if you can.

"Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

The best solution to your problem is to get a good scratching post for your cats.

If you get a scratching post for your cats, they likely will not use your sofa at all to sharpen their claws.

A god scratching post needs to be heavy so your cat is not able to move it. This means it must weigh 15-20 kilos or more. The scratching surface must be made of sisal or hemp rope so your cat can use its full strength when scratching.

One single cat claw can hold the cat's weight, so they are strong.

For your cats sitting on the sofa, you can use a folded towel for them to lie/sit on.

It's most probably a vocalization of his excitement.

Barking is not always something negative or aggressive. Compare it to a human screaming: it can be someone screaming in rage or frustration, or it could be a child screaming in joyful play.

It could also be his way of broadcasting his presence to any potential intruder or his dog-friends in the neighborhood. His way of saying "Here I am."

Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

An emergency is any sudden, serious problem. If you're unsure, call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. They can tell you whether to come in.

Go immediately if your pet:
- Has trouble breathing, breathes with the mouth open (cats), or has blue or very pale gums
- Is bleeding heavily
- Collapses, is unresponsive, or has a seizure
- Ate something poisonous
- Was hit by a vehicle or fell, even if they seem fine
- Is straining to pee with nothing coming out (especially male cats)
- Has a swollen belly and keeps retching (dogs)
- Suddenly acts very differently from normal

Save your vet's number and the nearest 24-hour clinic in your phone today, and know the route.

This is an emergency. Ibuprofen can kill cats, and cats are far more sensitive to it than dogs. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. Don't wait for signs.

Signs can start within a few hours:
- Brown or muddy-coloured gums
- Fast or deep breathing, weakness
- Swelling of the face or paws
- Vomiting, or yellow eyes and gums

Before you go:
- Bring the medicine pack and note when it happened and how many tablets may be missing.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't give milk, food or any other medicine.

On the way, keep her calm in a carrier with good airflow. Keep all medicines where pets can't reach them.

I have never heard this before and can't find any reliable information to back it up, nor does it make any sense.

I could find no vet on record as saying that it could cause a problem. Multiple sites dedicated to investigating such kinds of claims found it to also be false (notably Snopes and Hoax Slayer.) There is simply no verifiable or reliable evidence that ice water causes bloat.

Bloat is a real condition and drinking too fast is a possible cause, so the closest it could come would be if your dog drank faster because the water was colder, it could potentially be problematic, but not directly due to being ice water or ice cubes.

Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

Don't waste any more time, but take him to a vet! Animals are tough on themselves. By the time you realize they are in pain, they are in SERIOUS pain. Take him to the vet to find out whats going on. Even if you can't afford an expensive surgery at least the vet can find a humane way to help him.

Often, yes. Section 6 of RA 9482 tells the Department of Agriculture to lead free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs, with priority for high-risk, low-income areas. LGUs must fund vaccines and run registration and vaccination (Section 7).

Executive Order No. 84 (1999) also calls for mass dog vaccination with free vaccines every March, Rabies Awareness Month.

Schedules differ by place, so watch for announcements from your barangay or ask your city or municipal veterinary office about the next free vaccination drive.

Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.
